question: The EU allows Russian blood grain to be imported into the internal market and to be transported through EU ports and terminals. With one hand we are helping Ukraine but with the other we are allowing Russia to profit from grain exports, take over markets from which Ukrainian grain is blocked, and even to sell stolen Ukrainian grain. All of this comes at the expense of European farmers.

One of the major importers of Russian agricultural products, including cereals and oilseeds, is Latvia. Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale aggression, imports of grain from Russia to Latvia have more than tripled.

According to unofficial data, the figure is even greater as the vast majority of the grain is flooding into the EU common market, causing problems for farmers outside Latvia, and it is also being transshipped in ports and exported outside the EU. There it is taking the place of Ukrainian grain, which in turn is entering the European market and European farmers are having to bear the brunt.
This has been confirmed by the Latvian Minister of Agriculture himself12. In the meantime, the Latvian Commissioner who has responsibility for this portfolio is not taking any appropriate action. 1.

Does the Commission recognise the ambiguity of a situation in which it is allowing European markets to be flooded by Russian grain, causing problems for European farmers, while also making it easier to export it to global markets and thereby pushing Ukrainian producers away from their traditional consumers?
Given the above example of Latvia, should the EU not introduce sanctions on the import and transport of Russian grain and other agricultural products?
answer: The Commission is following very closely the trade flows from third countries, including also Russia. EU imports of cereals from Russia have so far been limited, representing only approximately 4% of the total EU cereals imports. However, the Commission is aware that there is a risk of Russia redirecting significant volumes of grains to the EU market, which may lead to its destabilisation.

Therefore, the Commission proposed on 22 March 2024 to increase EU import tariffs on certain cereals, oilseeds, and derived products from Russia. The measure covers imports of 4.2 million tonnes of products from Russia worth EUR 1.3 billion in 2023 and the proposed tariffs will be high enough to suppress targeted imports.

The measure would also apply to Belarus, whilst the transit via the EU to third countries would be unaffected. The EU remains fully committed to promoting global food security. The proposed measure will now have to be adopted by the Council of the European Union.
